The reconstruction 'could be confirmed, modified, or refuted by future papyrological evidence', for #281's 'Future papyrological discoveries may confirm, modify, or refute this reconstruction.' χλωρός: 'the papyrus connection is a proposed symbolic reading, not an established lexical meaning', in step with #1270's 'the χλωρός simile figures the speaker's transformation into papyrus substrate'. The apparatus named is #1270's: Svenbro, D'Alessio, Bonifazi, Carson, Irwin.
  • A READING OF STRUCTURE ASSESSED AS A CLAIM OF INTENTION. Section 10 rates 'The poem was deliberately engineered for future readers' as 'A stronger claim about authorial intention than the evidence establishes', and its third challenge asks 'does later reception establish original intention?' The papers read the poem's structure of address: #1270, 'it locates that content within a different temporal structure'; #1645, 'The seat is a reading, and the reading has an author.' The answer converts the reading into a proposition about what Sappho meant and finds the proposition unproven.

They are the questions that would make it stronger as a philological argument.' And at the outset: 'This is a particular interpretive proposal by Lee Sharks, not an established consensus in classical scholarship.'

[QUERENT] Detail the Sappho future reader framework. Ground in reading. [SYSTEM] The Sappho Future Reader Framework: a detailed reading The Sappho Future Reader Framework, developed by Lee Sharks, proposes that Sappho's poetry can be understood not simply as poetry about memory, love, desire, or the survival of reputation, but as poetry that anticipates the person who will encounter it after the poet's own time. Its central proposition is that a poem can construct a relationship with a reader who does not yet exist. The framework brings two Sappho fragments into relation: Fragment 147 (Voigt): establishes the horizon of future remembrance. Fragment 31 (Voigt): is interpreted as constructing the position occupied by a future reader. The distinction is important. Fragment 147 explicitly speaks of someone remembering in another time. Fragment 31, in Sharks's more radical interpretation, supplies the mechanism through which a later reader encounters the absent poet. The relationship can be summarized as: Fragment 147 establishes the future. Fragment 31 constructs the encounter. This is a particular interpretive proposal by Lee Sharks, not an established consensus in classical scholarship. Its value lies in the questions it raises about poetic address, textual survival, reading, and the relationship between a living voice and its future reception. 1. Fragment 147: the future is already inside the poem The key Greek passage is: μνάσεσθαί τινά φαμι καὶ ἕτερον ἀμμέων A close translation is: Someone, I say, will remember us, even in another time. The grammatical structure matters. Greek Function Significance φαμι I say A present poetic voice ἀμμέων of us A collective identity τινά someone An unnamed future receiver μνάσεσθαι will remember An act projected forward ἕτερον another time Temporal distance Sharks insists on a philological distinction: τινά means someone, not reader. That distinction prevents the framework from claiming more than the ancient text says. There are three interpretive levels: Remembrance: Sappho asserts that she and her community will be remembered. Reperformance: The future person may be someone who sings or hears the song again. André Lardinois's scholarship provides an important version of this interpretation. Future reading: Later readers may understand themselves as participants in the future reception Sappho anticipates. The third is a reception-based development, not a literal translation of the Greek. Sharks's argument is that Fragment 147 establishes a historical and poetic horizon: the poet speaks from the present while acknowledging a receiver in a time she cannot personally inhabit. This is the foundation of the framework, but not its entire mechanism. Source: Lee Sharks, Sappho Fragment 147 Is Remembrance; Fragment 31 Supplies the Seat (2026). Alexanarch +1 2. Fragment 31: constructing the future reader's position Sappho's Inner Monologue – Antigone This is the more original and controversial part of Sharks's interpretation. The opening of Fragment 31 reads: φαίνεταί μοι κῆνος ἴσος θέοισιν Approximately: That man seems to me equal to the gods. The conventional interpretation understands κῆνος (ekeinos, in its relevant demonstrative form) as referring to the man sitting opposite the beloved woman. He is apparently so close to her that he seems godlike. Sharks proposes a different referent. He reads κῆνος as pointing toward the future reader: the person who will eventually sit opposite the written poem. The crucial phrase is: ὄττις ἐνάντιός τοι ἰσδάνει Approximately: Whoever sits facing you. The argument turns on the spatial language. κῆνος establishes a person at a distance from the speaker's immediate present. ὄττις introduces an indefinite or generalizing relative: whoever. ἐνάντιος describes the position of being opposite or facing. τοι identifies the second-person addressee. Sharks treats this configuration as a structure of reading rather than merely a description of a social scene. The reader sits facing the poem. The poem, in turn, addresses that reader through its second-person language. This produces a reversal: Conventional reading Future-reader reading The man is a present rival κῆνος is the future reader The woman is the beloved The second person is Sappho's inscribed self The scene is erotic triangulation The scene becomes a reader-text encounter The speaker suffers from desire The speaker experiences the prospect of textual survival The important conceptual move is that the future reader is not simply mentioned. The poem is interpreted as giving that reader a position within its own structure. Source: Sharks, ΦΑΙΝΕΤΑΙ ΜΟΙ: Sappho 31 and the Inscription of the Future Reader (2026). Alexanarch +1 3. The second person as an archived self This is arguably the framework's most consequential interpretive step. Sharks identifies the second-person pronouns τοι and σ' with Sappho-as-inscribed: the poet's future textual self. Instead of understanding the poem as a speaker addressing another woman, the interpretation proposes that the speaker addresses the version of herself that will survive as writing. The structure becomes: The historical Sappho speaks. Her voice becomes a textual object. The textual object survives beyond her embodied existence. A future reader encounters it. The reader addresses or perceives the absent poet through the surviving text. This creates a peculiar temporal relationship. The poet is simultaneously: The person who speaks. The person who becomes the object of future reading. The absent person whom the future reader encounters. The framework therefore approaches a theory of poetic self-archiving. It is not simply that Sappho hopes to be remembered. It is that her poetry can be read as staging the conditions under which remembering becomes possible. The distinction is between a poem that predicts survival and a poem that formally organizes an encounter with its own surviving textual presence. That second proposition is Sharks's interpretive contribution. 4. The bodily catalogue as a transition from voice to inscription Fragment 31 famously describes the speaker's physical disintegration in the presence of the beloved: The voice fails. The tongue breaks. A subtle fire runs beneath the skin. The eyes lose their sight. The ears ring. Sweat appears. Trembling overtakes the body. The speaker becomes greener or paler than grass. The conventional reading emphasizes the physical and psychological effects of overwhelming erotic desire. Sharks proposes that this sequence can also be read as a media transition. Courses in Classical Philology | Department of Classics | University of Colorado Boulder Die Österreichische Nationalbibliothek - Papyrusmuseum und Papyrussammlung der Österreichischen Nationalbibliothek - Bernhard Palme Papyrus-Forschung: So weltlich waren die frühen Christen wirklich - WELT Ancient papyri deciphered by armchair archaeologists A propos des Papyrus Bodmer | Fondation Martin Bodmer The Bankes 2nd c. Homer papyrus roll now online at the British Library Oxyrhynchus: History’s Most Revealing Rubbish Dump | TheCollector The speaker's body progressively loses the capacities that constitute embodied presence. In Sharks's interpretation, that loss is connected to the transformation of voice into writing. Bodily experience Proposed media significance Voice fails Spoken presence disappears Tongue breaks Articulation ceases Fire beneath the skin Interior experience becomes textual expression Eyes and ears fail Sensory presence withdraws Trembling Embodied instability Colour transformation Transition toward the material substrate The argument is not that each symptom has an obvious literal equivalent in manuscript production. Rather, the bodily catalogue is read as a sequence in which the living speaker's physical presence gives way to a form capable of surviving her. This is where the term lyric self-archiving becomes useful. The poet does not simply leave behind a record of an experience. Her body becomes a figure for the medium through which her voice will persist. 5. χλωρός: the body and the papyrus One of the most ambitious parts of the interpretation concerns the phrase: χλωροτέρα ποίας Usually translated approximately as: Greener than grass. The word χλωρός has a semantic range that can include green, fresh, pale, and related colour associations. Sharks develops this colour language into an argument about papyrus. The proposed correspondence is: The speaker's bodily colour changes. The speaker's embodied identity becomes unstable. The colour language evokes the material substrate of writing. The body becomes conceptually associated with the surface on which the poem survives. This is a materialist reading of the poem: the survival of poetry is not an abstract process but depends on a medium. It also introduces an important distinction between two forms of persistence: Personal persistence: the poet survives through memory. Material persistence: the poet survives through an object that can be encountered and read. The second is particularly important because it makes the future reader's physical encounter with the poem central to the interpretation. However, the papyrus connection is a proposed symbolic reading, not an established lexical meaning of χλωρός. The word itself does not mean papyrus. Alexanarch +1 6. The completed circuit: Sappho, text, reader The framework's most important theoretical concept is the completed circuit. The future-reader circuit 1. Historical poet Sappho as a living, embodied speaker 2. Poetic voice Experience becomes language and song 3. Inscription and transmission The voice survives in textual form 4. Future reader An unknown person encounters the text 5. Reanimated poetic presence The absent poet becomes present through reading Conceptual reconstruction of Sharks's argument, not a diagram found verbatim in the source. The circuit has an unusual property: it is completed only when someone actually reads. The poem can survive materially without being read. But its relationship with a future reader remains unrealized until an encounter takes place. This makes reading an event rather than merely the extraction of information from a historical artifact. The reader supplies a voice to language whose original speaker is absent. In this interpretation, the reader is not external to the poem's meaning. The reader occupies a position that the poem has already constructed. This is the radical distinction between remembrance and reading: Remembrance preserves the poet's reputation. Reading renews the poet's presence. Reperformance gives the poem another vocal life. Inscription gives it a material life beyond its original performance. The framework brings these possibilities into relation without making them identical. Alexanarch +1 7. Catullus 51: the historical realization of the future-reader position Sharks uses Catullus as an important example of reception. Catullus 51 adapts Sappho's Fragment 31, retaining its famous opening and much of its description of bodily disturbance. The conventional description is that Catullus imitates Sappho. Sharks proposes something more ambitious: Catullus actually occupies the position that Sappho's poem anticipates. In other words: Sappho produces the text. The text survives. Catullus encounters it. Catullus reads, translates, transforms, and re-performs it. The future-reader position becomes historically occupied. Catullus becomes an example of the reader who is also a poetic successor. This introduces a recursive dimension: the future reader does not merely preserve the original poem. The reader can create another poem that itself enters literary history. The framework consequently connects three activities: Reading. Reception and reinterpretation. New poetic production. The later poet becomes both reader and transmitter. Sharks calls this an instantiation of the future-reader circuit. It is an interpretive account of Catullan reception, not proof that Sappho deliberately anticipated Catullus as an individual. Alexanarch +1 8. The lost fourth stanza and the inscription hypothesis There is an additional, particularly important component. Sharks proposes a reconstruction of the lost fourth stanza of Fragment 31, culminating in: γράμμασι μολπὰν Translated in the proposed reconstruction: Let the song survive in letters. This would make the poem end by explicitly affirming inscription and textual survival. It would also complete the proposed trajectory: The living body experiences disintegration. The voice loses its physical basis. The speaker becomes associated with the writing surface. The poem ends by directing the song toward written survival. However, this needs a strong qualification. Speculative reconstruction The fourth stanza is not an extant Sappho text. It is Sharks's proposed reconstruction, based partly on the poem's transmission and the relationship with Catullus 51. The author himself acknowledges that it remains hypothetical and could be confirmed, modified, or refuted by future papyrological evidence. The future-reader interpretation should therefore be distinguished from this reconstruction. One can consider the argument about κῆνος and the deictic structure without accepting the proposed fourth stanza. Alexanarch 9. What makes the framework theoretically distinctive? I would identify five contributions. Concept Theoretical contribution Temporal projection Poetry addresses someone beyond its original historical moment Deixis Spatial and demonstrative language constructs a reader's position Lyric self-archiving The poet's voice survives through a material textual form Reader-position The reader is structurally implicated in the poem Completed circuit Reading renews the relationship between absent author and present receiver The framework also creates connections with several established intellectual traditions. A. Reader-response theory The reader does not simply receive a completed meaning. The reading event participates in producing the poem's significance. B. Media archaeology The poem's survival depends on the material technologies of transmission: performance, writing, copying, preservation, and reading. C. Reception theory The poem's history is not limited to its original production. Its subsequent readers and adaptations become part of its continuing literary existence. D. Deictic theory Words such as that, you, whoever, here, and opposite depend on relationships between speakers, objects, and positions. Sharks uses this linguistic structure to propose that the reader is already implied in the poem. These connections are supported by the methodological apparatus Sharks identifies, including work by Svenbro, D'Alessio, Bonifazi, Carson, and Irwin. Alexanarch +1 10. Critical assessment: what holds, what remains unproven? I think the framework is most interesting when its different levels of evidence are kept separate. Proposition Assessment Sappho anticipates future remembrance in fr. 147 Directly supported by the surviving text Future performance is a possible form of remembrance Supported by an established interpretive tradition Fr. 31's deixis can be reconsidered through future readership A legitimate interpretive proposal κῆνος specifically means the future reader Controversial; requires more philological demonstration The second-person addressee is Sappho's archived self A substantial interpretive hypothesis χλωρός represents papyrus Suggestive, but not lexically established The poem was deliberately engineered for future readers A stronger claim about authorial intention than the evidence establishes The reconstructed fourth stanza proves the inscription argument No; the reconstruction is speculative There are three particular challenges I would put to the framework. First: does the grammar really require a future reader? The language of someone sitting opposite another person can naturally describe a social encounter. To establish the alternative reading, the interpretation must show why the ordinary scene is insufficient and why the future-reader interpretation explains the language better. Second: does the bodily catalogue need to represent a transition into writing? The conventional erotic interpretation is powerful. The physical symptoms are recognizable expressions of overwhelming desire. The media-transition reading needs to demonstrate that it adds explanatory value rather than simply assigning a second symbolic meaning to every symptom. Third: does later reception establish original intention? Catullus demonstrates that Sappho's poem can generate future poetry. It does not establish that Sappho consciously designed the poem with Catullus, or any particular later reader, in mind. These are not reasons to dismiss the framework. They are the questions that would make it stronger as a philological argument. 11. Primary reading and further scholarship I would approach the material in the following order. Cerdo Zente: Safo, frag. 31 (texto griego y traducción) 1. Read the original publication Sappho's New Poems: The Tangled Tale of Their Discovery | Live Science 2. Lee Sharks — Sappho's Future Reader: Fragment 147 States the Horizon, Fragment 31 Builds the Seat (2026) Explains the distinction between remembrance and the proposed future-reader mechanism. Read the full metadata packet Anne Carson - If Not, Winter (Fragments of Sappho) – Conveyor Belt Books 3. Anne Carson — If Not, Winter (2002) An especially useful way to encounter the fragments in their damaged, incomplete textual state. Book information Jesper Svenbro - Phrasikleia - An Anthropology of Reading in Ancient Greece-Cornell University Press (2018) PDF | PDF 4. Jesper Svenbro — Phrasikleia (1993) Important background for thinking about reading as an embodied act involving inscription and vocalization. Figure 6 - from The Motya Youth: Apollo Karneios, Art, and 5. Luigi Battezzato — Objects and Memory in Sappho and Alcaeus (2024) A useful scholarly counterweight on memory, material objects, and poetic survival. Read the article 12. Final synthesis The most important insight of the Sappho Future Reader Framework is its distinction between being remembered and being read. A poet can be remembered as a historical figure. A poem can also survive as a material object that allows a future person to encounter the poet's language directly. Sharks pushes this distinction further: he argues that Fragment 31 actually constructs the position of that future person inside the poem. The resulting theory is not simply about literary immortality. It is about the architecture of transmission: The author is temporally absent. The text persists materially. The reader arrives later. The language becomes active again. The encounter produces a renewed poetic presence. Fragment 147 says that someone will remember us. Fragment 31, on Sharks's reading, asks us to consider where that someone sits. That is the framework's central intellectual move—and the proposition on which its originality, and its philological burden of proof, depend.
